name: Tariang
confidence_why: L-Thongkum (1997, 2002), the only first-hand source, never states a stress rule for Tariang but marks stress on the final (main) syllable of every sesquisyllable in her field transcriptions, and Sidwell & Jacq (2003) describe the same stressed-main-syllable pattern for West Bahnaric as a whole, so the reading is uncontradicted but rests on one fieldworker's notation rather than an explicit statement.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Implicit, from first-hand phonetic transcription rather than a prose rule: Tariang words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables of the shape CV(C)ˈCV(C); in every sesquisyllabic form the author places the IPA stress mark before the final (main) syllable, i.e. the presyllable is unstressed and stress is word-final. This matches the explicit family-level description in Sidwell & Jacq 2003:33-34 ('a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable.. Sesquisyllabism is typical for Bahnaric'). No Talieng-specific sentence of the form 'stress falls on X' was found in any accessible source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said; words are at most one minor + one main syllable in the data.
new_statements.exceptions: None. (1997:112 adds only that vowel length is not distinctive in Tariang.)
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms (isolated lexical items from fieldwork wordlists, Ban Dak Lan, Dak Chueng district); word-level; nothing on phrasal prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand data examined are Theraphan L-Thongkum's 'Tariang' recorded at Ban Dak Lan, Dak Chueng (Dakcheung) district, Sekong province, Laos (1997:111) = Glottolog tali1257 Talieng/Taliang [tdf]. Sidwell (2002:12 fn.3) states her Tariang 'is evidently the same language as Taliang discussed in Jacq & Sidwell 2000, and which we classified as a sister dialect of Kaseng'; Sidwell & Jacq (2003) treat 'Kasseng/Taliang' as one language (West Central Bahnaric). The 'Trieng' of the SIL Bangkok wordlist / Vietnamese Gie-Trieng [stg, Glottolog trie1243] is a different lect that patterns with West Bahnaric/Jeh-Halang (Sidwell 2002:12) and should not be conflated with tali1257.

new_statements.quote: [p. xxxvii] Phonological words in Bahnaric may be mono- or disyllabic, with the latter generally treated as sesquisyllablic (iambic stress). An illustrative example is Smith’s maximum word template for Sedang (1979:22): (CpVp)(Cm)Ci(Cm)V(G)(N)(Cf)(R) ... The vowels in stressed and unstressed syllables differ in their phonological status. Typically only a single non-contrastive vowel, usually schwa or conditioned variant, and a reduced consonant inventory occur in unstressed syllables, while the main syllables carry the full and rather large range of contrastive vowels and consonants. ... Like most Austroasiatic languages, the Bahnaric languages are not tonal, but many—such as Sedang—contrast two phonation types

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the statement held by the project (L-Thongkum 2002, PL-530 p.105 Table 9: Tariang kaˈlɛh, taˈkool.. = stress on the final/main syllable of sesquisyllables) and with the catalog's source; it adds the explicit words 'iambic stress' and 'not tonal', but only as a Bahnaric-wide generalization, not as a description of Tariang, so on its own it should not move the catalog kind from 'undetermined' to a language-specific determination. No contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Branch-level generalization only (no Tariang-specific statement anywhere in the work): Bahnaric words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables with iambic stress, i.e. an unstressed presyllable with a reduced (non-contrastive, schwa-like) vowel followed by a stressed main (final) syllable carrying the full vowel and consonant contrasts; the languages are not tonal (some have phonation-register contrasts). The work counts Taliang (Kasseng) = Tariang/Talieng/Trieng as (Central) Bahnaric, so the generalization is meant to cover it. The rest of the work is a bibliography plus language and author indexes; the Tariang-related entries (Diffloth 1991 handout; L-Thongkum 1997, 2001; Miller 1988 Trieng word list; Jacq & Sidwell 2000) carry no stress annotations.
new_statements.exceptions: none; monosyllabic words trivially bear the stress; phonation-type (register) contrasts noted for some Bahnaric languages (e.g. Sedang, North Bahnaric), not attributed to Tariang.
new_statements.identity_note: The work treats Tariang under the names Taliang (Kasseng) [Table 2, Central Bahnaric], 'Kasseng or Tareng' (ISO kgc, tgr), Talieng (tdf) and Trieng (stg), noting that Sidwell recommends merging all four as one language and that Ethnologue (2013) then classed Tareng and Kasseng as Katuic whereas Sidwell and Diffloth treat them as Bahnaric. No variety-specific phonological data for Tariang are given.
